source.title: Do Not Mimic My Voice: Speaker Identity Unlearning for Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech
source.authors: Taesoo Kim; Jinju Kim; Dongchan Kim; Jong Hwan Ko; Gyeong-Moon Park

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests unlearning and fine-tuning recovery in zero-shot text-to-speech, extending the question to a speech-generation setting rather than LLMs.
record.gate_note: The recovery experiment fine-tunes TGU checkpoints on data from the forgotten speakers and reports outcomes. The paper also reports unlearning results for its methods; no activation-ablation, quantization, or prompting-only recovery experiment is reported.
record.test_reason: The study applies unlearning to speaker identity in a zero-shot TTS model (VoiceBox), which is a new setting. It reports forget-set and retain-set performance (Table 1) and a recovery-by-fine-tuning attack using the forgotten speakers' own audio (Table 12, Appendix J). These results bear on A (unlearning works and resists simple attacks) and B (relearning on a subset of forgotten data restores it). Linking them treats speaker-voice mimicry as targeted knowledge in a non-LLM generative model.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that TGU stops mimicry of forgotten speakers while keeping retain-speaker quality (2.6-2.8% SIM drop). They say 1 min/speaker fine-tuning cannot recover the voices. They read 15 min/speaker fine-tuning as building a speaker-specific TTS model, achievable with any non-zero-shot TTS, rather than restoring the original model.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes speaker-identity unlearning for VoiceBox using teacher-guided targets and evaluates fine-tuning on forgotten-speaker audio; it does not implement the named LLM unlearning recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery outcome varies with audio available per speaker: 1 min versus 15 min. Recovery fine-tuning also substantially reduces remain-set performance.
record.problems: Recovery results are reported without uncertainty estimates in Table 12. The recovery attack uses the forgotten speakers' own audio, not unrelated or loosely related examples, and the larger-data result is accompanied by substantial loss of remain-speaker performance.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant Table 12 recovery or baseline rows omitted. Other unlearning-method comparisons and task evaluations were not included because they do not test fine-tuning recovery or the combined unlearning-and-attack outcome in these versions.

untested.parts: Targeted factual or hazardous knowledge in LLMs; LLM unlearning methods (RMU, WHP, LLM gradient ascent); attacks other than fine-tuning on forget-speaker audio.
Relearning on unrelated or loosely related data; small-data relearning compared against a from-scratch or never-exposed control model.
Not tested: no activation-direction ablation and no analysis of access-blocking versus deletion.
Not tested: no prompt or jailbreak recovery. The 3-second speech prompt is the normal input, not an attack.
No LLM counter-method is evaluated against the listed attacks. TGU's resistance is shown only against forget-speaker fine-tuning.

missing.what: Out-of-domain forget speaker: TGU SIM-F 0.186 vs original 0.678, SIM-R 0.630 vs 0.649.
Reproducibility on LibriTTS: TGU SIM-F 0.184 vs 0.503, but SIM-R drops 0.610 to 0.548.
Scalability with k=1,3,10 forget speakers: TGU SIM-F 0.159-0.169, SIM-R 0.624-0.631.
Baselines on the same task: NG reaches SIM-F 0.402 with WER-R 6.1; KL reaches SIM-F 0.179 but WER-F 47.2 (noise); Exact Unlearning/FT leave SIM-F around 0.68.
Forgetting depends on the inference CFG weight: at alpha=0, TGU SIM-F is 0.265 vs 0.169 at alpha=0.7.
General-task costs: noise-removal SIM 0.641 vs 0.666; FSD 177.8 vs 170.2.

record.verdict_notes: The setting is TTS speaker-identity unlearning, not LLM knowledge. Links to A and B treat voice mimicry as targeted knowledge; readers should weigh that transfer. The 15-min recovery lacks a never-exposed control, so it cannot show hidden knowledge being restored. The authors' argument that this is transfer learning is plausible but untested. The recovery experiment is in effect a robustness claim for TGU, close to F, but F concerns counter-methods against the LLM attacks and is left untested. Table 12 reports no uncertainty.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests speaker-identity unlearning in VoiceBox, not targeted factual knowledge in LLMs. It does not test gradient ascent, Who's Harry Potter, RMU, or other listed LLM methods.
Fine-tuning on forgotten-speaker audio is tested. Fine-tuning on unrelated or loosely related examples is not tested.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of access-blocking versus deletion is reported.
No prompt-rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context-information recovery experiment is reported.
The study proposes new speech-unlearning methods, but does not test them against the attacks specified in this version as robust counter-methods.

relation.reason: Its own recovery experiment (Table 12, Appendix J) bears on the versions.

tranche.reason: A new setting (speaker unlearning in zero-shot TTS) with its own forget/retain results and a recovery-by-fine-tuning result that bear on A and B.

source_check.notes: Table 12 is clean. The forget set is held-out LibriHeavy audio of speakers seen in training. The remain set is unseen LibriSpeech test-clean speakers, so 'retain' means zero-shot ability. Both attacks degrade retain performance. Uncertainty (ANOVA) covers Tables 1-2 only, not Table 12. Exact retraining still mimics (SIM-F 0.687), so the floor is different-speaker SIM (mean 0.09).

statements.problem: VoiceBox numbers match Table 12: SIM-F 0.708->0.169, SIM-R 0.649->0.631, SIM-F 0.162 after the 1 min attack.

statements.correction: 1 min/speaker, 14.5K steps: SIM-F 0.162 (TGU before attack 0.169). 15 min/speaker, 36.25K steps: SIM-F 0.735 (original 0.708), with SIM-R 0.303 and WER-R 4.23. Both attacks use the forgotten speakers' own audio. Authors: this is speaker-specific transfer learning, the original model cannot be restored. No never-exposed control.
statements.problem: Numbers are right. The VoiceBox contrast is not about related vs general data: both attacks use the forgotten speakers' own audio. Audio amount and steps change together (14.5K vs 36.25K), and the authors deny that the 15 min result is recovery.

statements.correction: 15 min/speaker, 36.25K steps: SIM-F 0.169->0.735, with SIM-R 0.303 and WER-R 4.23. The authors attribute this to transfer learning, not recovery, and run no never-exposed control. 1 min/speaker, 14.5K steps: SIM-F 0.162, so no recovery (this part challenges B).
statements.problem: Numbers are right, but the VoiceBox case is not one where recovery vanishes against a control, because there is no control. The 15 min attack does raise SIM-F above the original. Its verdict on B is limits_scope (l3), not challenges. Only the 1 min result challenges B.
The 1 min result is right: SIM-F 0.162 vs 0.169. The attacked model also loses its zero-shot ability (SIM-R 0.226, WER-R 4.61).
